subject: Seller financing — when to ask, how to structure
preheader: When sellers say yes · The 4 deal-types where it works · Why creative structures save deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Seller financing — when creative structures save the deal
marketSnapshot.body: Seller financing is when the seller acts as the lender, holding a note on the property. It's not rare; it's just under-asked-for. Works particularly well for long-time owners with significant equity who want to spread their capital-gains tax liability across multiple years, OR for properties that have sat on market and the seller is feeling holding costs. Done right, it can let you close deals you couldn't get conventional financing for, AND structure rate/terms better than market.

stats.label: When sellers most likely to agree

dealSpotter.address: Example: long-time owner, seller carry at favorable rate
dealSpotter.body: Property purchased originally 18+ years ago, owner wants out but doesn't want the tax hit of an outright sale this year. Structured: 5% down, 95% seller-financed at 6.0%, 7-year balloon. Compared to conventional 25% down at 6.8%: you keep ~20% of capital deployable elsewhere AND save 80bp on rate. The balloon is the only risk — plan a refinance path in years 5-7 from day one.

Conventional first mortgage covers 75% of purchase, seller carries a 15% second at interest-only for 5 years. You put down 10%. The second's payments don't include principal in years 1-5, which materially improves cash flow during the early hold. The seller benefits by spreading their tax exposure. Win-win structures like this are why being open to creativity expands your buy box.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Why are they offering 100% financing? · usually red flag
dealSpotter.body: Property listed by a wholesaler/operator offering 100% seller financing. The math looks amazing — zero capital deployed, immediate positive cash flow. The catch is usually one of: hidden tenant problems (non-paying tenant, eviction in progress), undisclosed deferred maintenance, or pricing 10-15% above market. Always ask 'why does the seller want this structure?' If you can't get a clear, plausible answer, the answer is bad. Walk.

blogFeature.title: Cap rate vs cash-on-cash vs DSCR — which metric actually matters?
blogFeature.excerpt: Seller-financed deals often optimize cash-on-cash dramatically by reducing capital deployed. The cap rate doesn't change, but the return on YOUR equity does.

qa.question: When does it make sense to ASK a seller for financing vs default to conventional?
qa.answer: Four scenarios where asking is reasonable. (1) The property has been on market 60+ days — the seller is feeling carrying costs and is open to creative solutions. (2) Long-time owner (5+ years) with significant equity AND known tax exposure — seller financing spreads their capital gains across multiple years. (3) You have strong negotiating cards (cash buyer, fast close, no inspection contingency) you can trade for favorable terms. (4) You'd otherwise not qualify or want to preserve conventional credit slots for other deals. The wrong scenarios: seller has a mortgage they need to pay off at sale (most do — they can't seller-finance), property is brand-new on market (seller hasn't felt pain), or structure introduces a balloon without a credible refinance plan.
